title: Short Stuff: Barbed Wire
summary: Short Stuff episode on barbed wire. The hosts open with a tall tale about John Warren "Bet a Million" Gates betting on whether Joseph Glidden's barbed wire could hold longhorn cattle, which they say may not be true. They explain that Glidden did not invent barbed wire, but patented a design that twisted a barb around wire and added a second wire to hold it in place, plus a method of mass production from his factory in DeKalb, Illinois. They discuss how barbed wire changed the American West: it made fencing cheap compared with wood or stone, ended open free-range grazing, hurt Native American nomadic life and free-range cattle, and worked alongside the Homestead Act of 1862 to concentrate land in fewer hands. They cover fence-cutting wars carried out by groups such as the Blue Devils, and the later military and wartime uses of barbed wire, including World War One and prisons.

segments.title: Opening banter and the Bet a Million Gates story
segments.summary: The hosts open with a playful, possibly apocryphal story of John Warren Gates betting that barbed wire could hold in longhorn cattle at a ranch in 1876.

segments.title: Joseph Glidden and the barbed wire patent
segments.summary: Glidden did not invent barbed wire but patented a design that twisted barbs onto wire with a second wire holding them in place, and he developed a method for mass production. His factory in DeKalb, Illinois produced about 263,000 miles of wire.

segments.title: How barbed wire changed the American West
segments.summary: Barbed wire made fencing cheap and fast compared with wood or stone, ending open free-range grazing and disrupting Native American nomadic life that had lasted thousands of years.

segments.title: Homestead Act, fencing and land concentration
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the Homestead Act of 1862 and fencing let homesteaders claim land, shrinking common grazing areas and concentrating land in fewer hands. Cattle also got caught in fences and died.

segments.title: Fence cutting wars and later uses of barbed wire
segments.summary: Groups such as the Blue Devils cut fences in fence cutting wars, which involved shootouts and deaths until authorities intervened. Barbed wire later appeared in World War One, prisons, and military use, and W. H. Olden wrote a poem about it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a joke about getting an infection and sign off the Short Stuff installment.
